parsed.summary: The R3 theorem is a faithful encoding of Fefferman's alternative (C). For every ν>0 it gives smooth, divergence-free, rapidly decaying initial data u₀ on ℝ³ and a smooth rapidly decaying force f such that no smooth (v,p) on ℝ³×[0,∞) exists with v(·,t)∈L² and uniformly bounded energy. The single most important caveat is in the periodic theorem: it is stated with ∀ u₀ f instead of ∃ u₀ f. It therefore asserts that every pair (u₀,f) is smooth, periodic and divergence-free and admits no solution, which is false (e.g. u₀ = 0, f = 0 is not excluded and has the zero solution). It is not the paper's Corollary 10.6.

glossary.plain: ∇·v(x) = trace of the Jacobian Dv(x); equals 0 if v is not differentiable at x
glossary.note: The junk value only arises at non-differentiable points; every use is paired with C^∞ hypotheses.

glossary.plain: f(x+e_i) = f(x) for all x and all coordinate unit vectors e_i
u₀ is C^∞ and divergence-free everywhere
In addition, for all m and K there is C with |∂^m u₀(x)| ≤ C/(1+|x|)^K
glossary.note: K is real; the base is ≥1, so rpow is well-behaved.

glossary.plain: All (x,t)-derivatives within ℝ^n×[0,∞) satisfy |∂^m f| ≤ C/(1+|x|+t)^K
f is smooth, 1-periodic in x for t≥0, and |∂^m f| ≤ C/(1+t)^K
(v,p) are C^∞ on ℝ^n×[0,∞) and satisfy: ∂_t v + (v·∇)v = νΔv − ∇p + f (one-sided t-derivative on [0,∞)), ∇·v = 0, and v(x,0) = u₀(x)
glossary.note: Smoothness rules out junk derivative values.

glossary.plain: Smooth solution with v(·,t) ∈ L² for each t≥0 and sup_t ∫|v|² < E for some E
glossary.note: The extra L² requirement only weakens (makes easier) the nonexistence claim.

glossary.plain: Smooth solution with v and p 1-periodic in x for all t≥0

lean_claims.plain: For every ν>0 there exist u₀: ℝ³→ℝ³ and f: ℝ³×ℝ→ℝ³ such that: u₀ is smooth, divergence-free and Schwartz-decaying; f is smooth on ℝ³×[0,∞) with all derivatives decaying like (1+|x|+t)^{-K}; and there are no smooth (v,p) on ℝ³×[0,∞) solving NS with v(·,t)∈L² and uniformly bounded energy.
For every ν>0 and EVERY u₀, f: u₀ is smooth, periodic and divergence-free; f is smooth, periodic and time-decaying; and no smooth periodic solution exists. This is false as stated.

paper_claims.plain: For every ν>0 there are f ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ³×(0,∞)) and u₀ = 0 such that the smooth solution on [0,1) has bounded energy and ‖u(t)‖_∞ → ∞ as t↑1. Hence no smooth bounded-energy global solution exists: alternative (C).
For every ν>0 there is a smooth periodic force, compactly supported in time, with zero initial velocity, for which no global smooth periodic solution exists: alternative (D).

coverage.why: Existential over data satisfying Fefferman's conditions, plus nonexistence of a smooth bounded-energy solution; u₀ = 0 and f ∈ C_c^∞ satisfy the decay conditions.
The Lean statement quantifies ∀ u₀ f instead of ∃ u₀ f; that universal claim is false, while the paper claims existence.

flags.explanation: The statement uses ∀ (u₀) (f) where alternative (D) and the paper require ∃. As written it claims every function u₀ is smooth, periodic and divergence-free. It also claims that for u₀ = 0, f = 0 no solution exists, but (v,p) = (0,0) is a solution. The statement is false and does not formalize the paper's corollary. It is a different (unprovable) claim, not merely a stronger one.
flags.probe_idea: Prove ¬ (∀ ν>0, ∀ u₀ f, InitialVelocityConditionPeriodic u₀ ∧ ...) by instantiating u₀ = fun x => x (not periodic), or u₀ = 0, f = 0 with solution v = 0, p = 0.

flags.explanation: The solution class additionally requires v(·,t) ∈ L² for each t. This adds requirements inside ¬∃, so the theorem is slightly weaker than 'no bounded-energy smooth solution'. It is harmless, since bounded energy for a measurable v essentially implies L², and it matches Fefferman (7).

lint_verdicts.why: Divergence is only used on fields required to be C^∞, so fderiv is the true derivative.
The denominator (1+‖x‖)^K is positive, so no division by zero occurs.
u₀ is C^∞ by the same structure, so iteratedFDeriv is genuine.
1+‖x‖+t ≥ 1 for t ≥ 0, so the denominator is positive.
1+t ≥ 1 for t ≥ 0, so the denominator is positive.
The subtraction is in ℝ³, not ℕ, so there is no truncation.
velocity_smooth gives C^∞ on ℝ³×[0,∞), so the one-sided derivWithin and fderiv are genuine (unique differentiability on Ici 0).
The integrable field (MemLp 2) guarantees ‖v‖² is integrable, so the integral is not a junk 0; in a ¬∃ statement a junk value would only weaken the claim anyway.
